Abstract:
Advanced imaging tools are revolutionizing the diagnosis, treatment, and monitoring of medical conditions, offering unprecedented insights into live cell behavior and biophysical markers. We introduce a modular, hand-held fluorescent microscope featuring rapid set-up and sub-millimeter resolution for real-time biological analysis. We apply our system to map pH and nitric oxide (NO), biomarkers central to wound healing, in subcutaneous wounds. Using machine learning to cluster pH reveals spatiotemporal trends, including a concentric gradient peaking at the center and stabilization at the wound edge. NO clustering shows high-concentration structures that decrease in size but intensify as healing progresses from hemostasis to proliferation, enabling prediction of the healing day and re-epithelialization. These biomarker mappings offer insights poised to inform future wound healing studies. This research lays the groundwork for integrating the modular imaging unit with bioelectronic devices in closed-loop feedback systems, using machine learning to guide optimal wound treatment and accelerate healing.

However, it is challenging to measure high-resolution 3D contact geometry for a compact robot finger, to simultaneously meet optical and mechanical constraints. In this work, we present the GelSight Wedge sensor, which is optimized to have a compact shape for robot fingers, while achieving high-resolution 3D reconstruction. Abstract:
<jats:p>This article presents the development of a volume measurement system for calibrating material flow in the print head of a 3D printer operating with FDM technology, with usage of pellet material. To ensure high printing precision, it was necessary to design a measurement system capable of calibrating material flow by determining the volume of the deposited material path. A laser triangulation method – an optical, non-contact distance measurement technique – was employed for this purpose. In this approach, diffused laser light, focused through a lens, is projected onto a CCD or CMOS sensor. The position of the laser beam on the sensor allows for the precise calculation of the distance to the object. Given the high cost of commercial laser profilometers and the closed architecture of low-cost systems offered by existing 3D printer manufacturers, a custom measurement solution was developed. The system architecture is based on low-cost an widely accessible materials. A dedicated image processing algorithm was developed to analyze the deformation of the laser line and convert the profile data into volumetric measurements. The system interfaces with the printer’s control unit. Experimental validation was conducted using a reference object – a machined plate with a insertion of known dimensions. The results confirmed high measurement accuracy, with errors in the range of tenths of a cubic millimeter, which is considered sufficient for the intended application.</jats:p>

Abstract:
This document describes an approach to develop a fully distributed multipurpose autonomous flight system. With a set of hardware, software, and standard flight procedures for multiple unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV), it is possible to achieve a relative low-cost plug and play fully-distributed architecture for multipurpose applications. The resulting system comprises an OptiTrack motion capture system, a Pixhawk flight controller, a Raspberry Pi companion computer, and the Robotic Operating System (ROS) for internode communication. The architecture leverages a secondary PID controller with the use of MAVROS, an open-source Python plugin for ROS, for onboard processing and interfacing with the flight controller. Featuring a procedure that receives the position vector from Optitrack System and returns the desired velocity vector for each time-step. This facilitates ease of integration for researchers. The result is a reliable, easy to use an autonomous system for multipurpose engineering research. To demonstrate its extensiveness, this paper shows experiments of a robotics navigation experiment utilizing the fundamentals of Markov Decision Processes (MDP) running at 60Hz, Wireless and with a network latency below 2ms. This paper reasons why fully distributed systems should be embraced as it maintains the reliability of the system with lower cost and easier implementation for the ground station. Combined with an intelligent choice approach for developing software architecture, it encourages and facilitates the use of autonomous systems for transdisciplinary research.

Abstract:
Deaf-blindness forces people to live in isolation. At present, there is no existing technological solution enabling two (or many) deaf-blind people to communicate remotely among themselves in tactile Sign Language (t-SL). When resorting to t-SL, deaf-blind people can communicate only with people physically present in the same place, because they are required to reciprocally explore their hands to exchange messages. We present a preliminary version of PARLOMA, a novel system to enable remote communication between deaf-blind persons. It is composed of a low-cost depth sensor as the only input device, paired with a robotic hand as the output device. Essentially, any user can perform hand-shapes in front of the depth sensor. The system is able to recognize a set of hand-shapes that are sent over the web and reproduced by an anthropomorphic robotic hand. PARLOMA can work as a “telephone” for deaf-blind people. Hence, it will dramatically improve the quality of life of deaf-blind persons. PARLOMA has been presented and supported by the main Italian deaf-blind association, Lega del Filo d'Oro. End users are involved in the design phase.

  Dynamic 3D thermal point clouds generated from a camera array system hold

significant potential for various applications, particularly in monitoring structural

deformations and thermal variations. These point clouds are especially beneficial in

mapping heat loss across structures, which is crucial for energy efficiency assessments

and environmental studies. Furthermore, they enhance non-destructive testing methods

for structures by providing detailed thermal and structural information that is not visible

to the naked eye.

  This study introduces a simplified method for creating dynamic 3D thermal point

clouds that effectively capture both the geometric deformations and temperature

fluctuations of observed objects. By leveraging multiple camera arrays, this approach

synthesizes data from RGB cameras with thermal infrared (TIR) imaging to produce

high-resolution 3D thermal maps. The resulting dynamic point cloud not only maintains

the spatial density and resolution of the RGB point cloud but also enriches it with critical

temperature attributes. This integration allows for a comprehensive visualization of heat

distribution and structural integrity in real-time.

  One of the key advantages of this methodology is that it obviates the need for

additional depth-sensing equipment, such as LiDAR or specialized depth cameras, which

are traditionally used for generating 3D point clouds and require complex registration

processes. Instead, this technique utilizes a straightforward calibration and alignment

process between the RGB and TIR images to model the environment accurately. This not

only simplifies the setup but also reduces the cost and complexity involved in deploying

engineering, building management, and environmental monitoring.

  In general, the approach is most effective for objects that possess rich, distinctive

features, which facilitates the successful application of Structure from Motion (SfM)

techniques. The fundamental limitation of SfM is its dependency on identifying and

matching common feature points across multiple images; without these, generating

accurate point clouds is challenging. This issue is particularly pronounced in scenarios

involving objects with smooth, featureless surfaces, or those that have repetitive patterns

which confuse feature detection algorithms. Moreover, SfM is highly sensitive to lighting

conditions. Optimal lighting is crucial for capturing clear, well-defined images required

for identifying feature points. Poor lighting can result in high noise levels and low

contrast in images, which substantially degrades the quality of feature detection and

matching. Under dim lighting conditions, or in cases where the object surfaces reflect

light unevenly, the effectiveness of SfM can be significantly compromised.

  Objects with complex geometries and rich textural details are more suited to this

technique as these characteristics provide a plethora of unique feature points for SfM

algorithms to utilize. In contrast, objects with smooth, reflective, or translucent surfaces

often fail in SfM processes because they lack sufficient feature points, and their surfaces

may cause reflections or refractions that confuse the image capture process.

This model is a volumetric fusion-based architecture that processes synchronized multi-view 2D

for choosing FasterVoxelPose lies in its compatibility with distributed system design: the model

explicitly accepts 2D heatmaps as input, making it possible to decouple the feature extraction stage

(on edge devices) from the 3D inference stage (on the server). This separation enables scalable

deployment across multiple edge units and minimizes bandwidth requirements, as heatmaps are

significantly more compact than raw images or video frames.

    In addition to its architectural suitability, FasterVoxelPose demonstrated competitive perfor-

mance in terms of both inference time and accuracy across different numbers of camera views,

and other State-of-the-art (SOTA) metrics.

    Alternative models were considered, such as approaches based on Plane Sweep Stereo by Lin

and Lee [11], a depth estimation technique commonly used for 3D reconstruction from multiple

views. However, such models were ultimately excluded due to several limiting factors. First, Plane

Sweep Stereo exhibits a monolithic architecture that tightly couples image processing, depth rea-

soning, and triangulation, making it significantly more difficult to distribute across heterogeneous

devices. Second, it incurs substantial computational overhead and latency, rendering it unsuit-

able for real-time applications with strict timing requirements. These constraints conflict with the

system’s design goals of scalability, low-latency inference, and modular deployment.

   To facilitate extensibility and future development, the system was implemented in a modular

and decoupled manner. Both the 2D heatmap extraction component and the 3D pose estimation

module are encapsulated as interchangeable components. This allows researchers and developers

to easily integrate alternative models in the future, whether for improving performance, reducing

inference cost, or accommodating new hardware capabilities. As more efficient or accurate models

are developed in the field of human pose estimation, they can be incorporated into the system with

minimal architectural changes.

    In summary, the selection of ResNet and FasterVoxelPose reflects a design philosophy grounded

in practical deployment considerations, real-time performance, and architectural modularity. This

combination allows for accurate and efficient 3D pose estimation while maintaining a flexible and

future-proof system structure.

    2.4. Pterodactyl Payload
   Developed by one of the teams in the NEBP leadership, Pterodactyl stands for Payload To
Enable Recording Of Data and Communication Telemetry Y(While) Lofted. The purpose of the
Pterodactyl flight computer is to record data from the balloon launch onto an onboard SD card so
that it can be reviewed after the payload is recovered. The sensors on Pterodactyl capture a variety
of data types including time/date (down to the second), coordinates, altitude, internal and external
temperatures, pressure, velocity/acceleration, and orientation/angular velocity. The electronic
components used in the pterodactyl are ublox M9N GPS, MS5611 Pressure Sensor, Sparkfun
OLED Screen, 10k Ohm Thermistor, and BNO055 Internal Measurement Unit.

   When the project was introduced to our team in the spring of 2023, the computer was already
assembled; however, there were some issues that came up. First, the onboard OLED screen was
broken, making setup without the use of an external computer impossible. This was an easy fix as a
new screen was ordered and it worked without problems. After that the thermistor broke which
caused multiple components of the device to not function properly. Once a new thermistor was
ordered and installed the device was once again functional. One of the biggest reoccurring issues
with the device was the length of time it took to acquire a signal from satellites. It could take
several minutes to acquire a signal; however, the M9N GPS that was being used should be able to
pick up a signal in a fraction of the time. It turned out that one of the components on the
pterodactyl was causing interference to the GPS. To fix this, the GPS was moved off the board and
connected with wires instead of plugging directly into the pterodactyl. Once this fix was
implemented the GPS performance improved drastically. Over the course of several months, the
pterodactyl code was updated by the creators to work better and some slight modifications were
made by our team to better cater to our needs, such as more specific coordinate values and easier
on device setup.

   During our testing in San Antonio, the Pterodactyl worked as intended as we obtained a data
file post launch from the onboard microSD card with the recorded information. According to the
file, the pterodactyl recorded data for 46 minutes and reached an altitude of over 59,000 feet before
it stopped recording. The file had a very large amount of data, so in the future it may be beneficial
to record data every couple of seconds instead of multiple logs per second in order to make the data
easier to navigate. This should be able to be done fairly easily by modifying the code.

    2.5. Webcam-based Video Streaming
   This video payload was not part of the ballooning payloads provided by the NEBP leadership
teams, but was implemented and tested as an optional payload for our team to incorporate
redundancy in real-time video streaming. This video streaming payload operates by recording
video from the Raspberry Pi Cameras and sending that data to a ground station via Rocket M5
radios. This process is facilitated through Linux-based script files, which manage video streaming
during the flight. A primary challenge in operating the video payload revolved around acquiring the
skills necessary in using Linux on the Raspberry Pi. This was essential for navigating the

Proceedings of the 2024 ASEE North Central Section Conference                                      9
Copyright © 2024, American Society for Engineering EducationRaspberry Pi file system, analyzing the system, and creating and editing script files for video
streaming. It also involved configuring the correct IP address on the Pi to ensure that the ground
station received video from the intended source. Understanding how the Raspberry Pi recognized
the cameras was another crucial aspect. We had encountered a few issues in how the Pi Cameras
were being recognized, which meant our script files applied to a different video port than the one
being assigned to the camera. Rectifying these issues allowed for our students to become more
skilled in navigating Linux and operating the Raspberry Pi effectively.

    Properly configuring the M5 radios was essential to stream video from the video payload to the
ground station. The access point M5 was connected to the video payload to go with the balloon
during a ballon flight. The data from the video payload was then transmitted to the second M5
attached to the ground station. The M5s needed to be configured so that they were able to properly
communicate and transmit data. The video scripts on the Raspberry Pi took the video from the Pi
Cameras and created a VLC video to be streamed to OBS on the ground station computer. It was

Abstract:
The SoLid experiment, short for Search for Oscillations with a Lithium-6 detector, is a new generation neutrino experiment which tries to address the key challenges for high precision reactor neutrino measurements at very short distances from a reactor core and with little or no overburden. The primary goal of the SoLid experiment is to perform a precise measurement of the electron antineutrino energy spectrum and flux and to search for very short distance neutrino oscillations as a probe of eV-scale sterile neutrinos. This paper describes the SoLid detection principle, the mechanical design and the construction of the detector. It then reports on the installation and commissioning on site near the BR2 reactor, Belgium, and finally highlights its performance in terms of detector response and calibration.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Climate change has been negatively impacting our environment. The adverse effects of
climate change include flooding, drought, rising sea levels, hurricanes, and high
temperatures in different regions. The primary source of climate change is the release of
greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. Methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), and carbon
dioxide (CO2) are examples of greenhouse gases. Specific human activities contribute to
the emission of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. Fossil fuel combustion is the
primary human activity responsible for greenhouse gas emissions. Carbon dioxide is the
most prevalent greenhouse gas, accounting for approximately 75% of global emissions.
This dominance of carbon dioxide in greenhouse emissions necessitated the concept of
carbon literacy to educate individuals and organizations on ways to reduce their carbon
footprint.
Robot-assisted digital storytelling is a digital storytelling method that uses social robots to
tell a story to audiences. From elementary schools to universities, robot-assisted
storytelling has been demonstrated to be an effective teaching method. However, no
published model exists for developers to create robot storytelling instruction or training.
Hence, this thesis proposes a robot-assisted digital storytelling model for carbon literacy
training. The study employed the design science research methodology for its activities.
The model development process started with the selection of articles that had been
published on robot storytelling. The selected articles were analyzed, and the procedures
and activities used to create robot storytelling were identified. Those activities and
procedures were synthesized to develop the proposed robot storytelling model. The
model was experimented with by using it to create digital storytelling, which trained
selected undergraduate students on carbon literacy. Similar training was delivered to
some students using a narrated PowerPoint presentation for comparison. The two pieces
of training were evaluated, and it was discovered that though both trainings improved
learning outcomes and motivation, the robot storytelling enhanced the participants'
knowledge of carbon literacy better than the narrated PowerPoint presentation. In
conclusion, this study proposed a six-element model that enhances learner motivation,
engagement, and learning outcomes in carbon literacy training.</jats:p>

Abstract:
We present a synchronized multisensory dataset for accurate and robust indoor localization: the Lund University Vision, Radio, and Audio (LuViRA) Dataset. The dataset includes color images, corresponding depth maps, inertial measurement unit (IMU) readings, channel response between a 5G massive multiple-input and multiple-output (MIMO) testbed and user equipment, audio recorded by 12 microphones, and accurate six degrees of freedom (6DOF) pose ground truth of 0.5 mm. We synchronize these sensors to ensure that all data is recorded simultaneously. A camera, speaker, and transmit antenna are placed on top of a slowly moving service robot, and 89 trajectories are recorded. Each trajectory includes 20 to 50 seconds of recorded sensor data and ground truth labels. Data from different sensors can be used separately or jointly to perform localization tasks, and data from the motion capture (mocap) system is used to verify the results obtained by the localization algorithms. The main aim of this dataset is to enable research on sensor fusion with the most commonly used sensors for localization tasks. Moreover, the full dataset or some parts of it can also be used for other research areas such as channel estimation, image classification, etc. Our dataset is available at: https://github.com/ilaydayaman/LuViRA_Dataset

Q Ren. Dynamic thermal 3d point cloud generation using structure from motion. Unknown journal, 2024.

This excerpt describes a 14-Raspberry-Pi camera array using software/network synchronization rather than PTP or a hardware trigger. The Pis were connected by Cat 6e Ethernet to a managed switch, with one Pi acting as the server and 13 as clients; client NTP pool addresses were restricted to the server to keep synchronization on the local network. The text explains that NTP estimates clock offset and round-trip delay using timestamp measurements t0–t3, with offset θ = [(t1−t0)+(t2−t3)]/2 and delay δ = (t3−t0)−(t2−t1). Image-guided surgery (IGS) depends on accurate tracking of surgical instruments to provide real-time navigation relative to critical anatomical structures. Most contemporary IGS systems utilize stereo infrared cameras to track fiducial markers attached to surgical instruments. However, such commercial solutions are prone to occlusion and remain cost-prohibitive for many healthcare settings. This work demonstrates that a multi-camera tracking system using commodity hardware can achieve sub-millimeter accuracy while addressing fundamental limitations of existing commercial solutions. Our system employs a ring-shaped fixture equipped with multiple RGB cameras mounted on a surgical light. We evaluate two tracking methods with adaptive Kalman filtering: multi-view monocular pose fusion and multi-view triangulation. Both methods are assessed under varying occlusion levels and compared against a gold-standard stereo infrared camera system. Results show our system achieves median target registration errors of 0.64 mm for static point tracking and 0.73 mm for dynamic trajectory tracking, with accuracy degrading gracefully under occlusion. Compared to existing solutions, our open source system offers a cost-effective, robust alternative for resource-constrained environments. All designs, code, and data are available at https://nist.mni.mcgill.ca/. Disclaimer: all links will be live after acceptance.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Accurate spatiotemporal alignment of multi-view video streams is essential for a wide range of dynamic-scene applications such as multi-view 3D reconstruction, pose estimation, and scene understanding. However, synchronizing multiple cameras remains a significant challenge, especially in heterogeneous setups combining professional- and consumer-grade devices, visible and infrared sensors, or systems with and without audio, where common hardware synchronization capabilities are often unavailable. This limitation is particularly evident in real-world environments, where controlled capture conditions are not feasible. In this work, we present a low-cost, general-purpose synchronization method that achieves millisecond-level temporal alignment across diverse camera systems while supporting both visible (RGB) and infrared (IR) modalities. The proposed solution employs a custom-built LED Clock that encodes time through red and infrared LEDs, allowing visual decoding of the exposure window (start and end times) from recorded frames for millisecond-level synchronization. We benchmark our method against hardware synchronization and achieve a residual error of 1.34 ms RMSE across multiple recordings. In further experiments, our method outperforms light-, audio-, and timecode-based synchronization approaches and directly improves downstream computer vision tasks, including multi-view pose estimation and 3D reconstruction. Finally, we validate the system in large-scale surgical recordings involving over 25 heterogeneous cameras spanning both IR and RGB modalities. This solution simplifies and streamlines the synchronization pipeline and expands access to advanced vision-based sensing in unconstrained environments, including industrial and clinical applications.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Visible images have been widely used for motion estimation. Thermal images, in contrast, are more challenging to be used in motion estimation since they typically have lower resolution, less texture, and more noise. In this paper, a novel dataset for evaluating the performance of multi-spectral motion estimation systems is presented. All the sequences are recorded from a handheld multi-spectral device. It consists of a standard visible-light camera, a long-wave infrared camera, an RGB-D camera, and an inertial measurement unit (IMU). The multi-spectral images, including both color and thermal images in full sensor resolution (640 × 480), are obtained from a standard and a long-wave infrared camera at 32Hz with hardware-synchronization. The depth images are captured by a Microsoft Kinect2 and can have benefits for learning cross-modalities stereo matching. For trajectory evaluation, accurate ground-truth camera poses obtained from a motion capture system are provided. In addition to the sequences with bright illumination, the dataset also contains dim, varying, and complex illumination scenes. The full dataset, including raw data and calibration data with detailed data format specifications, is publicly available.

Abstract:
This paper presents the ShanghaiTech Mapping Robot, a state-of-the-art unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) designed for collecting comprehensive multi-sensor datasets to support research in robotics, Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM), computer vision, and autonomous driving. The robot is equipped with a wide array of sensors including RGB cameras, RGB-D cameras, event-based cameras, IR cameras, LiDARs, mmWave radars, IMUs, ultrasonic range finders, and a GNSS RTK receiver. The sensor suite is integrated onto a specially designed mechanical structure with a centralized power system and a synchronization mechanism to ensure spatial and temporal alignment of the sensor data. A 16-node on-board computing cluster handles sensor control, data collection, and storage. We describe the hardware and software architecture of the robot in detail and discuss the calibration procedures for the various sensors and investigate the interference for LiDAR and RGB-D sensors. The capabilities of the platform are demonstrated through an extensive outdoor dataset collected in a diverse campus environment. Experiments with two LiDAR-based and two RGB-based SLAM approaches showcase the potential of the dataset to support development and benchmarking for robotics. To facilitate research, we make the dataset publicly available along with the associated robot sensor calibration data: https://slam-hive.net/wiki/ShanghaiTech_Datasets

Abstract:
Achieving robust autonomy in mobile robots operating in complex and unstructured environments requires a multimodal sensor suite capable of capturing diverse and complementary information. However, designing such a sensor suite involves multiple critical design decisions, such as sensor selection, component placement, thermal and power limitations, compute requirements, networking, synchronization, and calibration. While the importance of these key aspects is widely recognized, they are often overlooked in academia or retained as proprietary knowledge within large corporations. To improve this situation, we present Boxi, a tightly integrated sensor payload that enables robust autonomy of robots in the wild. This paper discusses the impact of payload design decisions made to optimize algorithmic performance for downstream tasks, specifically focusing on state estimation and mapping. Boxi is equipped with a variety of sensors: two LiDARs, 10 RGB cameras including high-dynamic range, global shutter, and rolling shutter models, an RGB-D camera, 7 inertial measurement units (IMUs) of varying precision, and a dual antenna RTK GNSS system. Our analysis shows that time synchronization, calibration, and sensor modality have a crucial impact on the state estimation performance. We frame this analysis in the context of cost considerations and environment-specific challenges. We also present a mobile sensor suite `cookbook` to serve as a comprehensive guideline, highlighting generalizable key design considerations and lessons learned during the development of Boxi. Finally, we demonstrate the versatility of Boxi being used in a variety of applications in real-world scenarios, contributing to robust autonomy. Purpose Symptom-triggered crop protection acts only after damage is committed, and the intervention window has narrowed. This review reframes pre-symptomatic sensing from a detection problem into a closed decision loop, establishing the physiological lead time of a signal, set against its detection confidence and the latency of the response it can trigger, as the organizing principle for anticipatory, site-specific decision-making. Methods A systematic-narrative synthesis was conducted across major bibliographic databases through June 2026. Studies reporting pre-symptomatic capability under field or realistic conditions were retained and coded onto a coupled lead-time × confidence × actionability framework spanning sensing, inference, and actuation. Results Optical modalities were found to dominate the evidence base, while electrophysiological and volatile signals extended achievable lead time. Single modalities were insufficient to separate biotic from abiotic stress, motivating heterogeneous fusion. Edge inference and temporal onset forecasting remained immature, detection confidence was rarely quantified, and the sensing-to-actuation loop was seldom closed. Reported performance degraded sharply from laboratory to field, particularly in perennial and smallholder systems. Abstract:
We propose a system to capture nearly synchronous frame streams from multiple and moving handheld mobiles that is suitable for dynamic object 3D reconstruction. Each mobile executes Simultaneous Localisation and Mapping on-board to estimate its pose, and uses a wireless communication channel to send or receive synchronisation triggers. Our system can harvest frames and mobile poses in real time using a decentralised triggering strategy and a data-relay architecture that can be deployed either at the Edge or in the Cloud. We show the effectiveness of our system by employing it for 3D skeleton and volumetric reconstructions. Our triggering strategy achieves equal performance to that of an NTP-based synchronisation approach, but offers higher flexibility, as it can be adjusted online based on application needs. We created a challenging new dataset, namely 4DM, that involves six handheld augmented reality mobiles recording an actor performing sports actions outdoors. We validate our system on 4DM, analyse its strengths and limitations, and compare its modules with alternative ones.

Abstract:
Air-bearing platforms for simulating the attitude dynamics of satellites require highly accurate ground truth systems. Commercial off-the-shelf motion-capture systems are used for this scope, although they are complex and expensive. This paper shows a novel and versatile method to estimate the attitude of rotational air-bearing platforms using a monocular camera and sets of fiducial LED markers. The work proposes a geometry-based, iterative algorithm that is significantly more accurate than other literature methods that involve solving the perspective-[Formula: see text]-point problem. Additionally, autocalibration procedures to perform a preliminary estimation of the system parameters are shown. The developed methodology is deployed onto a Raspberry Pi 4 microcomputer and tested with an array of LEDs soldered on a custom printed circuit board. Data obtained with this setup are compared against simulations of the system to determine and validate its performance. The hardware setup is also validated against independent inclinometric and gyroscope sensor measurements. Simulation and test results show expected 1-sigma accuracies of 12 arcs and 37 arcs for about- and cross-boresight rotations of the platform, respectively, and average latency times of 6 ms.

Abstract:
High-precision virtual environments are increasingly important for various education, simulation, training, performance, and entertainment applications. We present HoloCamera, an innovative volumetric capture instrument to rapidly acquire, process, and create cinematic-quality virtual avatars and scenarios. The HoloCamera consists of a custom-designed free-standing structure with 300 high-resolution RGB cameras mounted with uniform spacing spanning the four sides and the ceiling of a room-sized studio. The light field acquired from these cameras is streamed through a distributed array of GPUs that interleave the processing and transmission of 4K resolution images. The distributed compute infrastructure that powers these RGB cameras consists of 50 Jetson AGX Xavier boards, with each processing unit dedicated to driving and processing imagery from six cameras. A high-speed Gigabit Ethernet network fabric seamlessly interconnects all computing boards. In this systems paper, we provide an in-depth description of the steps involved and lessons learned in constructing such a cutting-edge volumetric capture facility that can be generalized to other such facilities. We delve into the techniques employed to achieve precise frame synchronization and spatial calibration of cameras, careful determination of angled camera mounts, image processing from the camera sensors, and the need for a resilient and robust network infrastructure. To advance the field of volumetric capture, we are releasing a high-fidelity static light-field dataset, which will serve as a benchmark for further research and applications of cinematic-quality volumetric light fields.

Abstract:
Human action recognition has been widely used in many fields of life, and many human action datasets have been published at the same time. However, most of the multi-modal databases have some shortcomings in the layout and number of sensors, which cannot fully represent the action features. Regarding the problems, this paper proposes a freely available dataset, named CZU-MHAD (Changzhou University: a comprehensive multi-modal human action dataset). It consists of 22 actions and three modals temporal synchronized data. These modals include depth videos and skeleton positions from a kinect v2 camera, and inertial signals from 10 wearable sensors. Compared with single modal sensors, multi-modal sensors can collect different modal data, so the use of multi-modal sensors can describe actions more accurately. Moreover, CZU-MHAD obtains the 3-axis acceleration and 3-axis angular velocity of 10 main motion joints by binding inertial sensors to them, and these data were captured at the same time. Experimental results are provided to show that this dataset can be used to study structural relationships between different parts of the human body when performing actions and fusion approaches that involve multi-modal sensor data.

107   Animals and Surgical Procedures



108   Four male Long–Evans rats aged 5-8 months, weighing 450-600 gm were housed

109    individually on a 12:12 hr reversed light/dark cycle and habituated to daily handling over 2

110   weeks before surgery. All experiments were performed according to a protocol approved by

111    the Institutional Animal Ethics Committee of the Indian Institute of Science.



112    Custom-built hyperdrives having 16 tetrodes + 2 references were implanted over the right

113   hemisphere under surgical anesthesia (80 mg/kg ketamine + 10 mg/kg xylazine followed by

114   0.5-2% isoflurane for maintenance). The tetrodes targeted different parts of the hippocampal

115    formation in different rats: area CA1 of the hippocampus (2 rats), medial entorhinal cortex

116   (MEC) (1 rat), MEC and Lateral Entorhinal Cortex (LEC) (1 rat).



117   Training and Experimental Protocol



118   The rats recovered for 5-7 days after the surgery until their weights stabilized. During

119   subsequent training and recordings, the rats were food deprived and trained to forage for

120   food on a 1 m x 1 m black square platform. The neural recordings were performed in multiple

121    setups: a 5.5 m x 3 m room (henceforth referred to as ‘the large room’), half of this same

122   room, 2.75 m x 3 m, a circular track (diameter = 1 m), a linear track (length = 1 m) and the

123   square platform used for training. Neural signals were recorded wirelessly in all these

124    setups. For small setups (circular track, linear track, and square platform), a single Picamera

125    sub-unit and a commercial camera were used for position tracking while the rats foraged for

126    food. For the large room recordings, 8 Picamera sub-units covering the entire room with

129   Neural Data Recording Hardware



130   Recordings were performed using the Cheetah data acquisition system and Cube-64, a 64-

131   channel wireless transmitter (Neuralynx, Bozeman, MT, USA). A control computer ran the

132   data acquisition software and stored the acquired data (Figure 1a).



133   Video Cameras



134   The tracking system comprised 8 overhead Picamera sub-units (Figure 1a). Each sub-unit

135   had a Raspberry Pi camera module v1 (containing an OmniVision OV5647 ColorCMOS

136  QSXGA 5 MP sensor with f/2.9 aperture lens) connected to a Raspberry Pi 2 model B

137   computer (1 GB RAM, 900 MHz quad-core processor and 32 GB class 10 SD card)

138    (https://www.raspberrypi.org). We recorded video on each Picamera sub-unit at 640 x 480

139    resolution at 30 Hz with high temporal accuracy and no dropped frames over 4 hrs of

140    recording. The Picamera system could acquire at higher frame rates with high temporal

141   accuracy, but there were occasional frame drops (0.22% for 50 Hz and 0.31% for 60 Hz),

142   and thus we chose to acquire at 30 Hz. Each camera has a field of view of 2.43 m x 1.82 m

143   when mounted at a height of 2.8 m. The parallel architecture of the Picamera system, with

144   each Raspberry Pi camera recording video on its own Raspberry Pi computer independently

145    of others, makes it easily scalable without compromising temporal accuracy. The Picamera

146   Python library (https://picamera.readthedocs.io/) was used to acquire video data along with

147   timestamps from the cameras. Video recordings from the Picamera were displayed using a

148   composite video output port available on each Raspberry pi.

162   system



163   Each Raspberry Pi was connected via a DGS-1024D ethernet hub (D-Link, Taipei, Taiwan)

164    to the control computer and remotely operated over the network using PuTTY

166    In order to synchronize position tracking data (see below) acquired in these videos with

167    neural recordings, it is critical to know the time at which each frame was recorded. Default

168   video capture protocols do not record timestamps for each frame. The Picamera Python

169    library offers an option to save operating system clock time, but this option is prone to

170   inaccuracy in timestamping introduced by other processes competing for CPU resources. To

171   reduce this inaccuracy in frame timestamps, we modified the Picamera library. Since the

172   Raspberry Pi’s Graphics Processing unit (GPU) runs its own real-time operating system, it

177   TTL (Transistor-Transistor Logic) pulses generated using Arduino Uno REV3

180    1a). Timestamps for each TTL input on/off transition were logged on all the Raspberry Pi

181   computers and the data acquisition system. Difference between timestamps recorded on

182   each Raspberry Pi computer and the data acquisition system corresponding to the first TTL

183   on transition gives us the instantaneous temporal offset between these devices. This offset

184   was then subtracted from all subsequent frame timestamps of each video to convert their

185   timestamps to the data acquisition system’s temporal reference frame. Our recordings

187   data acquisition system for up to 4 hrs of recording. Regardless of the extent of drift,

188   subsequent TTL on/off transitions are used to correct drift of the Raspberry Pi clocks from

189    the data acquisition system clock.

583   temporal accuracy without dropping frames.



584    Correlated with the debate about the exact shape of theta phase precession, there is an

585   ongoing debate about the exact shape of the place field. The shape of the place field is

586     critical to the two competing models of theta phase precession: while the ramp excitation

587   model requires asymmetric place field with a slow increase in firing rate as the rat

588   approaches the location with peak firing rate and a rapid fall off in firing rate as the rat exits

589    the place field (Mehta et al. 2002), the oscillatory interference model requires a symmetric

590   place field (O’Keefe and Recce 1993; Burgess and O’Keefe 2011). While the criteria used

591    for defining the place field can affect the estimated asymmetry, precise position tracking, and

592    the consequent increased confidence in the exact shape of the place field can further help

593    resolve this question.



594    In summary, the Picamera system described in the present work satisfies all the criteria

595    desirable in an efficient tracking system for use with large and complex environments: easy

596    to use, adaptable, temporally accurate, low-cost, scalable, open-source and easily available.

597   The system overcomes the bottleneck on tracking animal behavior in large spaces, therefore

598   reducing the gap between the natural environments and experimental setup.

   LARK: A Low-Cost, Accurate, Occlusion-Resilient, Kalman
    Filter-Assisted Tracking System for Image-Guided Surgery

     George Siderisa,∗,1, Justin Creea,1, Andrew Stirlinga, Mamadou Lya, Étienne Légerb and D.
     Louis Collinsb

    A R T I C L E  I N F O            A B S T R A C T

       Keywords:                                      Image-guided surgery (IGS) depends on accurate tracking of surgical instruments to provide real-
       Image-Guided Surgery                            time navigation relative to anatomical structures. Commercial stereo infrared trackers are accurate but
        Optical Tracking                                 prone to occlusion and cost-prohibitive for many settings. This work presents LARK, a multi-camera
      Kalman Filtering                                      optical tracking system using commodity RGB hardware and multi-view redundancy and fusion.
       Multi-Camera Calibration                 We develop and evaluate two complete tracking methods: multi-view monocular pose fusion and
       Multi-View Triangulation                          multi-view triangulation. Both methods are assessed under varying occlusion levels using a precision-2026  Pose Estimation                               machined grid and an anatomical head phantom, and compared against a gold-standard stereo infrared
        Fiducial Markers                                  system. With five cameras and adaptive Kalman filtering, LARK achieves median target registration
                                                                errors of 0.64 mm for point localization with triangulation and 0.73 mm for trajectory tracking
                                                        with pose fusion on the machined grid. Camera-subset experiments show graceful degradation inOct                                                            adaptive pose-fusion accuracy as fewer views remain available. With tracking hardware costing under
6                                                 $1,000 USD, LARK provides a low-cost platform for image-guided surgery research. Hardware
                                                          designs and software are publicly available at https://nist.mni.mcgill.ca/software/, and datasets at
                                                            https://nist.mni.mcgill.ca/data/.

Onboard Synchronization
Each of our 50 Jetson AGX Xavier boards drives six cameras through a
Leopard Imaging adapter board. The adapter board provides hardware
shutter synchronization between the six cameras through a primary and
secondary configuration. One camera, set up as the primary camera,
triggers the other five camera shutters. This hardware synchronization
scheme ensures all cameras connected to the same Jetson AGX Xavier
board are capturing frames with microsecond accuracy. However, we
found that despite synchronized camera shutters, the encoded frames
could still be out of sync. Upon close examination of the associated
timestamps, we discovered the multithreaded encoding process intro-
duced a constant offset to the encoded frames’ timestamps because
threads are initialized sequentially. To correct this systematic error,

secondary configuration to ensure encoded frames on each Jetson AGX
Xavier board are in sync. There are six consumer threads initiated
on a Jetson AGX Xavier board to encode frames from each of the
six cameras. Each thread will request frames from its camera in the
order that the frame is captured. Each frame has a timestamp recording
the time it was captured. We set the primary camera as reference and
use the timestamp from its frame as a benchmark to synchronize the

From text 'ren2024dynamicthermal3d pages 33-39'.

Q Ren. Dynamic thermal 3d point cloud generation using structure from motion. Unknown journal, 2024.

The excerpt addresses network-based clock synchronization for a Raspberry Pi camera array, not an electrical synchronization signal or sensor-level hardware triggering system. It states that Raspberry Pi 4B does not support Precision Time Protocol (PTP), so Network Time Protocol (NTP) was used instead. Wi-Fi synchronization can produce differing clock accuracy because of signal conditions, latency, interference, packet loss, and obstructions; a wired local network is reported to provide lower delay, offset, and jitter. The described cluster contains 14 Raspberry Pis: one server and 13 clients, connected through a managed switch using Cat 6e Ethernet cables, with clients configured to use the server as their NTP source. This excerpt does not identify a five-Pi LARK Sideris system, does not state that the camera sensors use an XTR hardware trigger or another electrical trigger, and does not provide a measurable exposure skew or jitter value in the supplied portion. It also does not discuss CSI camera-cable length, signal integrity, or a CSI-cable-specific synchronization issue. The excerpt concerns temporal clock/network synchronization; it provides no information about spatial reconstruction errors, which should not be conflated with temporal exposure errors.

## pqac-00000053

From text 'ren2024dynamicthermal3d pages 27-33'.

Q Ren. Dynamic thermal 3d point cloud generation using structure from motion. Unknown journal, 2024.

The excerpt discusses synchronization problems in multi-camera systems but does not identify a LARK Sideris five-camera system specifically. It states that differing frame rates and trigger response times can prevent perfect synchronization. For Raspberry Pi camera arrays, parallel-SSH broadcasting is described as a possible control method, but manufacturing differences mean that each Raspberry Pi may operate its capture process at a slightly different clock speed, so images are not necessarily captured simultaneously. Precision Time Protocol (PTP) is mentioned as a preferred synchronization approach, but the Raspberry Pi 4B is said not to support PTP; the excerpt then begins introducing an alternative method, but the provided text ends before explaining it. The passage also describes an array of multiple pre-calibrated cameras for simultaneous multi-view capture, primarily to handle moving objects. It provides no exact statement about an electrical synchronization signal, sensor XTR hardware triggering, a five-Pi configuration, measurable exposure skew or jitter, or the length or limitations of CSI cables. The stated errors of 0.4, 0.1, and 0.8 pixels elsewhere in the excerpt are reprojection/alignment errors and should not be interpreted as temporal synchronization measurements.

From text 'saxena2018inexpensivescalablecamera pages 24-27'.

Rajat Saxena, Warsha Barde, and Sachin S. Deshmukh. Inexpensive, scalable camera system for tracking rats in large spaces. Journal of Neurophysiology, 120:2383-2395, Nov 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.1152/jn.00215.2018, doi:10.1152/jn.00215.2018. This article has 16 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt describes the Picamera system from Saxena et al., not the LARK Sideris five-Raspberry-Pi global-shutter system. It provides one explicit electrical synchronization detail: an Arduino sends TTL time-synchronization pulses to every Picamera sub-unit and the data-acquisition system. The described setup contains eight Raspberry Pi camera sub-units, rather than five. The excerpt also states that the system can acquire at 100 Hz with sub-millisecond temporal accuracy without dropping frames. It does not identify an XTR sensor hardware-trigger implementation, nor does it mention NTP or PTP network synchronization. It also gives no measured exposure skew, timing jitter, or CSI-cable length/associated issue. The temporal claims should therefore not be conflated with spatial tracking accuracy: the excerpt discusses synchronization and acquisition timing, while its nearby discussion of precise position tracking concerns spatial errors and place-field estimation.

{"answer": "## Short answer

**Yes for distributed Raspberry Pi camera arrays; not verified for the specified long-ribbon, shared-Pi arrangement.** A published build used Raspberry Pi cameras on networked Pis to generate dynamic 3D point clouds. A separate eight-Pi tracking system measured exceptionally close frame alignment, but tracked animals in **2D**, not 3D. In the sources examined, I could not verify a built 3D-tracking, motion-capture, or photogrammetry system connecting several cameras to *one* Pi with **bare CSI ribbon cables ≥0.5 m**. Nor did I find a measured maximum usable bare-ribbon length or cable-length-dependent image-error rate for such a system. (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000049)

| Build | Camera arrangement and purpose | Synchronization evidence | Cable evidence and limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Ren, *Dynamic Thermal 3D Point Cloud Generation Using Structure from Motion* (2024)** | Built a 14-Pi cluster—one server and 13 clients—and an array of **12 Raspberry Pi HQ RGB cameras plus one FLIR Boson thermal camera**. It reports reconstructed dynamic thermal 3D point clouds, including a hand and sand. | A local server supplied **NTP over wired Ethernet**; capture commands could be broadcast with parallel SSH. For the 13 listed wired clients, measured **NTP clock offsets** ranged from **−0.155 to +0.768 ms**, jitter from **0.016 to 0.941 ms**, and network delays from **0.061 to 0.181 ms**. Three Wi-Fi test Pis instead showed offsets of **−17.164 to −2.070 ms**, jitter of **1.869–15.420 ms**, and delays of **23.029–35.787 ms**. These are *clock/network statistics, not measured differences between camera exposure times*. The author considered PTP unavailable on the Pi 4B configuration used; no camera hardware trigger or exposure-skew test is reported. | Each Pi-to-switch **Cat 6e Ethernet cable was 1.5 m**. That is **not** a CSI ribbon length; the camera ribbons and their signal integrity were not characterized. The wired-versus-Wi-Fi problems reported were wireless congestion, interference, obstruction and packet loss—not CSI image corruption. (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000002) |
| **Saxena, Barde and Deshmukh, *Journal of Neurophysiology* (2018)** | Eight Raspberry Pi 2/Camera Module v1 units tracked rats across a 5.5 × 3 m arena. **Relevant engineering precedent, but 2D position tracking rather than 3D reconstruction.** | Network connections provided remote control, **not NTP camera synchronization**. An Arduino delivered common TTL pulses whose timestamps aligned Pi camera-frame timestamps to a data-acquisition clock; the paper does **not** establish that the TTL directly triggered all camera shutters. Camera starts were within **0.5 ms** in multiple sessions; subsequent frame times stayed within **0.5 ms**, with **<0.05 ms** separation in one illustrated four-hour recording. Reported clock drift relative to acquisition was **<13 µs** over up to four hours. At 30 Hz there were no dropped frames in four hours; at 50 and 60 Hz the reported drop rates were **0.22%** and **0.31%**, respectively. Inter-frame-interval jitter and inter-camera frame offset are distinct measurements. | One camera was attached to each Pi, but CSI cable length and cable-related errors were **not reported**. Figure 5a presents the across-camera frame-time comparison. (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000055) |
| **Sideris et al., LARK (October 2026 preprint)** | An actual five-camera, Raspberry-Pi-board/MIPI **global-shutter** instrument-tracking rig uses multiple views for 3D triangulation and pose fusion; it reports submillimetre *spatial* tracking errors. | The methods refer to cameras synchronized through an electrical signal, but the inspected text supplies **no quantified inter-camera exposure skew or jitter**. Its **0.64-mm** and **0.73-mm** results are *spatial registration errors*, not synchronization accuracies. | The inspected report does not specify ≥0.5-m CSI ribbons or a cable signal-integrity test. (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043) |

**What the ribbon-cable evidence actually says.** A documented conventional Pi-camera connection uses a **15-cm CSI ribbon**. A Pi-based single-camera 3D-print measurement project explicitly says ordinary CSI ribbons are only several centimetres long and instead uses **CSI-to-HDMI adapter boards and an HDMI cable** to place its camera farther away; it specifies neither that cable’s length nor a maximum reliable bare-CSI length. Another build lengthened ribbons for two cameras on an Arducam multiplexer but was a balloon-video system, **not 3D reconstruction**; its reported pixelation and lag arose from **video-transmission bandwidth**, not a demonstrated CSI electrical failure. None of those examples validates a ≥0.5-m bare ribbon carrying several cameras to one Pi. (pqac-00000056, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025)

**Important exclusions:** A photogrammetric underwater three-camera rig used a Pi Zero W to issue hardware triggers, but its **Basler cameras connected over Ethernet to a laptop**, not through Pi CSI ports. A 300-camera volumetric studio used a Pi as an **NTP server** while **Jetson** boards hosted the cameras; its measured **16.67-ms** camera-synchronization bound must not be presented as a Pi-camera result. A 100-Pi light-field array used one CSI camera per Pi but did not report NTP/PTP/trigger accuracy or CSI cable lengths, and its reported demonstration was computational refocusing rather than verified 3D motion capture. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030)

**Interpretation:** Ren establishes that a networked, one-Pi-per-view approach has produced 3D photogrammetric output; Saxena establishes a separate, well-measured hardware-*timestamp*-alignment approach. Ren’s sub-millisecond **NTP offsets do not prove sub-millisecond simultaneous exposures**. Conversely, the available literature does not establish that 0.5-m bare CSI ribbons are either reliable or impossible: the specific requested multi-camera 3D implementation and its cable-length/signal-integrity measurements remain unverified. (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000022)"}

state.question: Has anyone built a multi-camera 3D tracking, motion-capture or photogrammetry system from Raspberry Pi cameras in which either several cameras share one Raspberry Pi through CSI ribbon cables of about 0.5 m or longer, or each camera has its own Raspberry Pi synchronized over the network (NTP, PTP or a hardware trigger), and what frame-synchronization accuracy, cable-length limits or signal-integrity problems were reported?

answer.question: Has anyone built a multi-camera 3D tracking, motion-capture or photogrammetry system from Raspberry Pi cameras in which either several cameras share one Raspberry Pi through CSI ribbon cables of about 0.5 m or longer, or each camera has its own Raspberry Pi synchronized over the network (NTP, PTP or a hardware trigger), and what frame-synchronization accuracy, cable-length limits or signal-integrity problems were reported?
answer.answer:
Yes. ## Short answer

**Yes for distributed Raspberry Pi camera arrays; not verified for the specified long-ribbon, shared-Pi arrangement.** A published build used Raspberry Pi cameras on networked Pis to generate dynamic 3D point clouds. A separate eight-Pi tracking system measured exceptionally close frame alignment, but tracked animals in **2D**, not 3D. In the sources examined, I could not verify a built 3D-tracking, motion-capture, or photogrammetry system connecting several cameras to *one* Pi with **bare CSI ribbon cables ≥0.5 m**. Nor did I find a measured maximum usable bare-ribbon length or cable-length-dependent image-error rate for such a system. (ren2024dynamicthermal3d pages 33-39, ren2024dynamicthermal3d pages 46-53, saxena2018inexpensivescalablecamera pages 5-8, saxena2018inexpensivescalablecamera pages 15-18)

| Build | Camera arrangement and purpose | Synchronization evidence | Cable evidence and limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Ren, *Dynamic Thermal 3D Point Cloud Generation Using Structure from Motion* (2024)** | Built a 14-Pi cluster—one server and 13 clients—and an array of **12 Raspberry Pi HQ RGB cameras plus one FLIR Boson thermal camera**. It reports reconstructed dynamic thermal 3D point clouds, including a hand and sand. | A local server supplied **NTP over wired Ethernet**; capture commands could be broadcast with parallel SSH. For the 13 listed wired clients, measured **NTP clock offsets** ranged from **−0.155 to +0.768 ms**, jitter from **0.016 to 0.941 ms**, and network delays from **0.061 to 0.181 ms**. Three Wi-Fi test Pis instead showed offsets of **−17.164 to −2.070 ms**, jitter of **1.869–15.420 ms**, and delays of **23.029–35.787 ms**. These are *clock/network statistics, not measured differences between camera exposure times*. The author considered PTP unavailable on the Pi 4B configuration used; no camera hardware trigger or exposure-skew test is reported. | Each Pi-to-switch **Cat 6e Ethernet cable was 1.5 m**. That is **not** a CSI ribbon length; the camera ribbons and their signal integrity were not characterized. The wired-versus-Wi-Fi problems reported were wireless congestion, interference, obstruction and packet loss—not CSI image corruption. (ren2024dynamicthermal3d pages 33-39, ren2024dynamicthermal3d pages 39-46, ren2024dynamicthermal3d pages 46-53, ren2024dynamicthermal3d pages 27-33) |
| **Saxena, Barde and Deshmukh, *Journal of Neurophysiology* (2018)** | Eight Raspberry Pi 2/Camera Module v1 units tracked rats across a 5.5 × 3 m arena. **Relevant engineering precedent, but 2D position tracking rather than 3D reconstruction.** | Network connections provided remote control, **not NTP camera synchronization**. An Arduino delivered common TTL pulses whose timestamps aligned Pi camera-frame timestamps to a data-acquisition clock; the paper does **not** establish that the TTL directly triggered all camera shutters. Camera starts were within **0.5 ms** in multiple sessions; subsequent frame times stayed within **0.5 ms**, with **<0.05 ms** separation in one illustrated four-hour recording. Reported clock drift relative to acquisition was **<13 µs** over up to four hours. At 30 Hz there were no dropped frames in four hours; at 50 and 60 Hz the reported drop rates were **0.22%** and **0.31%**, respectively. Inter-frame-interval jitter and inter-camera frame offset are distinct measurements. | One camera was attached to each Pi, but CSI cable length and cable-related errors were **not reported**. Figure 5a presents the across-camera frame-time comparison. (saxena2018inexpensivescalablecamera pages 5-8, saxena2018inexpensivescalablecamera pages 15-18, saxena2018inexpensivescalablecamera pages 27-30, saxena2018inexpensivescalablecamera media ed0abd9e) |
| **Sideris et al., LARK (October 2026 preprint)** | An actual five-camera, Raspberry-Pi-board/MIPI **global-shutter** instrument-tracking rig uses multiple views for 3D triangulation and pose fusion; it reports submillimetre *spatial* tracking errors. | The methods refer to cameras synchronized through an electrical signal, but the inspected text supplies **no quantified inter-camera exposure skew or jitter**. Its **0.64-mm** and **0.73-mm** results are *spatial registration errors*, not synchronization accuracies. | The inspected report does not specify ≥0.5-m CSI ribbons or a cable signal-integrity test. (sideris2026larkalowcost pages 4-5, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 3-4, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 1-2, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 7-8) |

**What the ribbon-cable evidence actually says.** A documented conventional Pi-camera connection uses a **15-cm CSI ribbon**. A Pi-based single-camera 3D-print measurement project explicitly says ordinary CSI ribbons are only several centimetres long and instead uses **CSI-to-HDMI adapter boards and an HDMI cable** to place its camera farther away; it specifies neither that cable’s length nor a maximum reliable bare-CSI length. Another build lengthened ribbons for two cameras on an Arducam multiplexer but was a balloon-video system, **not 3D reconstruction**; its reported pixelation and lag arose from **video-transmission bandwidth**, not a demonstrated CSI electrical failure. None of those examples validates a ≥0.5-m bare ribbon carrying several cameras to one Pi. (parker2026establishingaformalised pages 93-98, zbroja2026laserbasedvolumemeasurement pages 2-3, dickinson2024engineeringexperiencesand pages 7-9, dickinson2024engineeringexperiencesand pages 9-11)

**Important exclusions:** A photogrammetric underwater three-camera rig used a Pi Zero W to issue hardware triggers, but its **Basler cameras connected over Ethernet to a laptop**, not through Pi CSI ports. A 300-camera volumetric studio used a Pi as an **NTP server** while **Jetson** boards hosted the cameras; its measured **16.67-ms** camera-synchronization bound must not be presented as a Pi-camera result. A 100-Pi light-field array used one CSI camera per Pi but did not report NTP/PTP/trigger accuracy or CSI cable lengths, and its reported demonstration was computational refocusing rather than verified 3D motion capture. (rofallski2020measuringartificialreefs pages 2-3, rofallski2020measuringartificialreefs pages 3-4, heagerty2024holocameraadvancedvolumetric pages 3-4, heagerty2024holocameraadvancedvolumetric pages 6-7, heagerty2024holocameraadvancedvolumetric pages 7-9, pschipsch2026nearfarwherever pages 3-4, pschipsch2026nearfarwherever pages 8-10)

**Interpretation:** Ren establishes that a networked, one-Pi-per-view approach has produced 3D photogrammetric output; Saxena establishes a separate, well-measured hardware-*timestamp*-alignment approach. Ren’s sub-millisecond **NTP offsets do not prove sub-millisecond simultaneous exposures**. Conversely, the available literature does not establish that 0.5-m bare CSI ribbons are either reliable or impossible: the specific requested multi-camera 3D implementation and its cable-length/signal-integrity measurements remain unverified. (ren2024dynamicthermal3d pages 33-39, ren2024dynamicthermal3d pages 39-46, ren2024dynamicthermal3d pages 46-53, saxena2018inexpensivescalablecamera pages 5-8, saxena2018inexpensivescalablecamera pages 15-18, zbroja2026laserbasedvolumemeasurement pages 2-3)

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a Raspberry Pi multi-device camera synchronization build intended to support synchronized image capture for Structure from Motion (SfM), and therefore potentially 3D photogrammetry. It uses a 14-unit Raspberry Pi cluster: one server Pi controls operations and gathers data from 13 client Pis. The devices are connected through a managed switch using wired Cat 6e Ethernet, with each Ethernet cable reported as 1.5 m long. PTP was considered but is unavailable on the Raspberry Pi 4B, so the system uses NTP. The clients are prevented from accessing public NTP servers; their NTP pool address is set to the server, keeping synchronization within the local network. The text states that wired NTP produces lower delay, clock offset, and jitter than Wi-Fi NTP, attributing this to more stable signaling and avoidance of wireless congestion and interference. It also reports that Wi-Fi conditions can create significant timing discrepancies and that a well-configured LAN can achieve millisecond-level or better NTP accuracy. However, the excerpt does not provide the actual numerical delay, offset, or jitter measurements from Tables 2 and 3. It also does not state the number of cameras explicitly, provide CSI ribbon-cable lengths, describe hardware triggering, or report camera signal-integrity measurements beyond general wired-network stability.

The text mentions Raspberry Pi Model 5 hardware, including its quad-core 2.4 GHz processor and second CSI interface, which can support two camera modules per device and potentially reduce the number of processing units. Communication is described as WiFi-based; the authors explicitly note that WiFi may introduce latency and limit use with dynamic scenes. It also gives no CSI ribbon-cable lengths, including exact 0.5 m or 1 m cables, and provides no analysis of CSI signal-integrity problems. Relevant limitations instead concern calibration accuracy, pose errors, lens distortion, camera-plane misalignment, occlusions, and thermal output in densely packed arrays. Future work includes more precise synchronization mechanisms, dynamic-scene analysis, and occlusion-aware models. No related-reference details about alternative 3D-reconstructing builds or ribbon lengths appear in this excerpt.

contexts.context: This excerpt describes a 14-Raspberry-Pi camera array using software/network synchronization rather than PTP or a hardware trigger. contexts.context: The excerpt describes synchronization challenges for both a dual RGB/TIR camera system and a multi-camera Raspberry Pi array. For the dual-camera setup, perfect synchronization is difficult because the cameras have different frame rates and trigger-response times. For the Raspberry Pi array, cameras can be controlled using the Python parallel-ssh package, which broadcasts capture commands to predefined Raspberry Pi IP addresses. The excerpt identifies Precision Time Protocol (PTP) as a potentially appropriate synchronization method, but explicitly states that the Raspberry Pi 4B does not support PTP, motivating an alternative approach. contexts.context: The excerpt identifies Saxena et al. (2018) as presenting an open-source, low-cost, scalable multi-camera animal-tracking system called the Picamera system. The system comprises eight overhead Raspberry Pi cameras and was used with wireless electrophysiology to track rats in environments up to 16.5 m²; the demonstrated large arena was 5.5 m × 3 m. The article’s stated advantage is substantially better temporal accuracy than a commercial tracking system, improving alignment of videos from multiple cameras and estimation of spatial firing and head-direction characteristics. The excerpt contrasts this with conventional 4K cameras, which generally cannot log timestamps for every frame and therefore require a temporal synchronization signal such as an LED flash; synchronization accuracy using that method is limited by camera frame rate. However, these pages do not specify the Picamera system’s network-based or hardware-trigger synchronization mechanism, measured camera-frame timing error, CSI cable lengths, or signal-quality measurements. snippets: We developed and benchmarked an open-source, scalable multi-camera tracking system based on low-cost hardware.
This “Picamera system” was used in combination with a wireless recording system for characterizing neural correlates of space in environments of sizes up to 16.5 m2.
The Picamera system showed substantially better temporal accuracy than a popular commercial system.
Here, we describe a novel tracking system comprising 8 overhead Raspberry Pi cameras
Typical 4k cameras do not have a provision to log timestamps for each frame and thus need to use temporal synch signal (LED flash) to align with the neuronal recording system.
Accuracy of the LED synchronization method is limited by the frame rate.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns HoloCamera rather than the LARK Sideris five-Raspberry-Pi global-shutter camera system, so it does not establish LARK-specific synchronization hardware, sensor XTR triggering, CSI-cable limitations, or exposure skew. It does provide a potentially comparable two-tier synchronization design: six cameras on each Jetson AGX Xavier board use a primary camera to trigger five secondary cameras electrically through a hardware shutter-synchronization connection, while software timestamp matching corrects encoding offsets. Across 50 Jetson boards, the system uses a Raspberry Pi as a local NTP server; reported network-clock measurements were under 0.5 ms round-trip delay, under 0.1 ms clock offset, and under 0.1 ms jitter. The article also states that capture signals were dispatched across 300 cameras with sub-millisecond precision and that hardware synchronization provides microsecond accuracy for cameras on the same board. However, the excerpt does not identify PTP, does not quantify actual sensor exposure skew or exposure-start jitter after camera acquisition begins, and does not discuss CSI cable length or related signal-integrity issues. The reported values therefore should not be attributed to LARK or used as evidence about its temporal performance.

The only quantitative camera-related specifications supplied concern image and video performance, including 5-megapixel still images, 1080p at 30 fps, 720p at 60 fps, and 640×480 video at 60/90 fps. Therefore, this excerpt cannot substantiate a documented 15 cm or several-centimeter standard, a practical maximum CSI-ribbon length, or any universal maximum. It should not be used to infer such limits or to conflate the bare CSI ribbon with Ethernet or HDMI cabling.
contexts.question: Locate any quantitative firsthand Raspberry Pi CSI camera flat ribbon cable length ≥0.5 m and signal errors / artifacts (especially Crawford bee tracking, stereo / 3D) in retrieved texts; separate 1.5m CAT6 Ethernet and HDMI adapter lengths from bare CSI ribbon; cite documented standard 15cm or several cm and practical limit, without inventing universal maximum.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Has anyone built a multi-camera 3D tracking, motion-capture or photogrammetry system from Raspberry Pi cameras in which either several cameras share one Raspberry Pi through CSI ribbon cables of about 0.5 m or longer, or each camera has its own Raspberry Pi synchronized over the network (NTP, PTP or a hardware trigger), and what frame-synchronization accuracy, cable-length limits or signal-integrity problems were reported?

Yes. ## Short answer

**Yes for distributed Raspberry Pi camera arrays; not verified for the specified long-ribbon, shared-Pi arrangement.** A published build used Raspberry Pi cameras on networked Pis to generate dynamic 3D point clouds. A separate eight-Pi tracking system measured exceptionally close frame alignment, but tracked animals in **2D**, not 3D. In the sources examined, I could not verify a built 3D-tracking, motion-capture, or photogrammetry system connecting several cameras to *one* Pi with **bare CSI ribbon cables ≥0.5 m**. Nor did I find a measured maximum usable bare-ribbon length or cable-length-dependent image-error rate for such a system. (ren2024dynamicthermal3d pages 33-39, ren2024dynamicthermal3d pages 46-53, saxena2018inexpensivescalablecamera pages 5-8, saxena2018inexpensivescalablecamera pages 15-18)

| Build | Camera arrangement and purpose | Synchronization evidence | Cable evidence and limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Ren, *Dynamic Thermal 3D Point Cloud Generation Using Structure from Motion* (2024)** | Built a 14-Pi cluster—one server and 13 clients—and an array of **12 Raspberry Pi HQ RGB cameras plus one FLIR Boson thermal camera**. It reports reconstructed dynamic thermal 3D point clouds, including a hand and sand. | A local server supplied **NTP over wired Ethernet**; capture commands could be broadcast with parallel SSH. For the 13 listed wired clients, measured **NTP clock offsets** ranged from **−0.155 to +0.768 ms**, jitter from **0.016 to 0.941 ms**, and network delays from **0.061 to 0.181 ms**. Three Wi-Fi test Pis instead showed offsets of **−17.164 to −2.070 ms**, jitter of **1.869–15.420 ms**, and delays of **23.029–35.787 ms**. These are *clock/network statistics, not measured differences between camera exposure times*. The author considered PTP unavailable on the Pi 4B configuration used; no camera hardware trigger or exposure-skew test is reported. | Each Pi-to-switch **Cat 6e Ethernet cable was 1.5 m**. That is **not** a CSI ribbon length; the camera ribbons and their signal integrity were not characterized. The wired-versus-Wi-Fi problems reported were wireless congestion, interference, obstruction and packet loss—not CSI image corruption. (ren2024dynamicthermal3d pages 33-39, ren2024dynamicthermal3d pages 39-46, ren2024dynamicthermal3d pages 46-53, ren2024dynamicthermal3d pages 27-33) |
| **Saxena, Barde and Deshmukh, *Journal of Neurophysiology* (2018)** | Eight Raspberry Pi 2/Camera Module v1 units tracked rats across a 5.5 × 3 m arena. **Relevant engineering precedent, but 2D position tracking rather than 3D reconstruction.** | Network connections provided remote control, **not NTP camera synchronization**. An Arduino delivered common TTL pulses whose timestamps aligned Pi camera-frame timestamps to a data-acquisition clock; the paper does **not** establish that the TTL directly triggered all camera shutters. Camera starts were within **0.5 ms** in multiple sessions; subsequent frame times stayed within **0.5 ms**, with **<0.05 ms** separation in one illustrated four-hour recording. Reported clock drift relative to acquisition was **<13 µs** over up to four hours. At 30 Hz there were no dropped frames in four hours; at 50 and 60 Hz the reported drop rates were **0.22%** and **0.31%**, respectively. Inter-frame-interval jitter and inter-camera frame offset are distinct measurements. | One camera was attached to each Pi, but CSI cable length and cable-related errors were **not reported**. Figure 5a presents the across-camera frame-time comparison. (saxena2018inexpensivescalablecamera pages 5-8, saxena2018inexpensivescalablecamera pages 15-18, saxena2018inexpensivescalablecamera pages 27-30, saxena2018inexpensivescalablecamera media ed0abd9e) |
| **Sideris et al., LARK (October 2026 preprint)** | An actual five-camera, Raspberry-Pi-board/MIPI **global-shutter** instrument-tracking rig uses multiple views for 3D triangulation and pose fusion; it reports submillimetre *spatial* tracking errors. | The methods refer to cameras synchronized through an electrical signal, but the inspected text supplies **no quantified inter-camera exposure skew or jitter**. Its **0.64-mm** and **0.73-mm** results are *spatial registration errors*, not synchronization accuracies. | The inspected report does not specify ≥0.5-m CSI ribbons or a cable signal-integrity test. (sideris2026larkalowcost pages 4-5, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 3-4, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 1-2, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 7-8) |

**What the ribbon-cable evidence actually says.** A documented conventional Pi-camera connection uses a **15-cm CSI ribbon**. A Pi-based single-camera 3D-print measurement project explicitly says ordinary CSI ribbons are only several centimetres long and instead uses **CSI-to-HDMI adapter boards and an HDMI cable** to place its camera farther away; it specifies neither that cable’s length nor a maximum reliable bare-CSI length. Another build lengthened ribbons for two cameras on an Arducam multiplexer but was a balloon-video system, **not 3D reconstruction**; its reported pixelation and lag arose from **video-transmission bandwidth**, not a demonstrated CSI electrical failure. None of those examples validates a ≥0.5-m bare ribbon carrying several cameras to one Pi. (parker2026establishingaformalised pages 93-98, zbroja2026laserbasedvolumemeasurement pages 2-3, dickinson2024engineeringexperiencesand pages 7-9, dickinson2024engineeringexperiencesand pages 9-11)

**Important exclusions:** A photogrammetric underwater three-camera rig used a Pi Zero W to issue hardware triggers, but its **Basler cameras connected over Ethernet to a laptop**, not through Pi CSI ports. A 300-camera volumetric studio used a Pi as an **NTP server** while **Jetson** boards hosted the cameras; its measured **16.67-ms** camera-synchronization bound must not be presented as a Pi-camera result. A 100-Pi light-field array used one CSI camera per Pi but did not report NTP/PTP/trigger accuracy or CSI cable lengths, and its reported demonstration was computational refocusing rather than verified 3D motion capture. (rofallski2020measuringartificialreefs pages 2-3, rofallski2020measuringartificialreefs pages 3-4, heagerty2024holocameraadvancedvolumetric pages 3-4, heagerty2024holocameraadvancedvolumetric pages 6-7, heagerty2024holocameraadvancedvolumetric pages 7-9, pschipsch2026nearfarwherever pages 3-4, pschipsch2026nearfarwherever pages 8-10)

**Interpretation:** Ren establishes that a networked, one-Pi-per-view approach has produced 3D photogrammetric output; Saxena establishes a separate, well-measured hardware-*timestamp*-alignment approach. Ren’s sub-millisecond **NTP offsets do not prove sub-millisecond simultaneous exposures**. Conversely, the available literature does not establish that 0.5-m bare CSI ribbons are either reliable or impossible: the specific requested multi-camera 3D implementation and its cable-length/signal-integrity measurements remain unverified. (ren2024dynamicthermal3d pages 33-39, ren2024dynamicthermal3d pages 39-46, ren2024dynamicthermal3d pages 46-53, saxena2018inexpensivescalablecamera pages 5-8, saxena2018inexpensivescalablecamera pages 15-18, zbroja2026laserbasedvolumemeasurement pages 2-3)

info.query: Has anyone built a multi-camera 3D tracking, motion-capture or photogrammetry system from Raspberry Pi cameras in which either several cameras share one Raspberry Pi through CSI ribbon cables of about 0.5 m or longer, or each camera has its own Raspberry Pi synchronized over the network (NTP, PTP or a hardware trigger), and what frame-synchronization accuracy, cable-length limits or signal-integrity problems were reported?
